name: Ben Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing English literature and history, which most people at home think is a nice hobby, not a degree. A normal week is four lectures, two seminars and a lot of reading in the library, plus three mornings pulling coffees at a cafe near the station. My dad's an electrician and my mum works in a council office. I live in a flat share with a medic and a chemist, and they work twice as hard as me. I use AI now and then to check my referencing, but I wouldn't let it write anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. New tools come along, a few people get excited, and then things settle. I'd say that to my dad, who's been hearing about robots taking trades since the nineties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit relieved, because a lot of my worry is about whether a humanities degree is worth the loan. If AI only does routine stuff, then writing and thinking still have a place. I'd still wonder if employers value it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the cafe and the reading and aim for a teaching or publishing route. I'd apply for a summer internship at a local publisher, and join the student paper. I'd also put aside fifty pounds a month, because my loan covers fees but not the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy. My degree isn't a straight line to a job, so I always carry some doubt, plan or no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a plateau make your degree feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, yes, but not safe. People still ask me what I'll do with an English degree, and a plateau doesn't answer that. I'd need to show I can write, research and speak, and a CV that proves it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the cafe job give you that the degree doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cafe gives me cash and people skills. Nobody in my flat believes a barista job teaches anything, but I learn to handle rude customers and rush hour. That's worth more than a lot of the courses I've seen.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**, since new tools come, people get excited and things settle.
I'd tell my dad, who has heard about robots taking trades since the nineties.
think: A plateau means writing and thinking still have a place, but I still wonder if **employers** value my degree.
A lot of my worry is the **loan**.
do: Keep the **cafe job** and aim for teaching or publishing.
Apply for a summer **internship** at a local publisher and join the student paper.
feel: **Fine**, a bit uneasy, because my degree isn't a straight line to a job.
S0.quote: People still ask me what I'll do with an English degree, and a plateau doesn't answer that.
fieldNote: Worry is about the **worth of a degree**, not about AI itself.
Values the cafe job for people skills, a practical streak from his electrician father.
Uses AI lightly and with boundaries.

steps.text: Keep three weekly mornings at the station cafe
Apply for a summer internship at a local publisher
Put fifty pounds a month aside beyond the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fair worry and people should take it seriously, but not panic. I'd mention it in seminars, because half my course acts like it's a distant thing. And I'd say humanities graduates have always had to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit rattled. If AI takes over a lot of writing, checking and planning, then communications and publishing jobs shrink. Teaching might survive better, because classrooms need people. I'm moving that way in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into a postgraduate teaching course, and shadow a teacher at my old school for a week. I'd also learn the AI tools properly so I'm not the only one who can't. I'd take a coding or data module as an extra. And I'd cut a night at the pub each week to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. I've got options, but they're all narrower than before, and I'm not sure which one is best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Writing is on the list of tasks AI takes first. How does that land for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad says tradespeople are the last ones to be replaced, and he'd laugh about me studying books. But he'd be kind about it. He'd say get a skill, and maybe he's right. I might do the electrical apprenticeship if I really had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your dad have a view on this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A teaching job would be steady, though the pay is not great. Publishing is the dream, but there'd be fewer places. I'd rather aim for something with a person in the room, because those jobs seem the hardest to shrink.

say: I'd say it's a **fair worry** and people should take it seriously but not panic.
I'd say humanities graduates have always had to adapt.
think: Communications and publishing jobs shrink, while **teaching** might survive because classrooms need people.
I'm already moving that way in my head.
do: Look into a **teaching** course and shadow a teacher at my old school.
Learn the **AI tools** properly so I'm not the only one who can't.
Take a coding or **data module** as an extra.
feel: A bit **anxious**, with more options but all narrower than before.
S1.quote: I'd rather aim for something with a person in the room, because those jobs seem the hardest to shrink.
fieldNote: Shifts from publishing to **teaching** because the scenario hits writing first.
Dad's trade is a real fallback, which gives him a quiet floor.
Public line is measured; private line is rattled.

steps.text: Shadow a teacher at my old school for a week
Take a data module alongside the English degree
Practise with AI tools on my essay planning
Skip one pub night a week to save

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an emergency plan, and quick. Governments need to pay people to retrain, and universities need to tell students what's coming. I wouldn't be calm online. I'd write something for the student paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be gutted. Full AGI by 2028 would mean writing, research and teaching materials are done by machines. Graduating in 2029 would feel like finishing a race after the stadium has been demolished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a serious conversation with my parents about whether to stay. If I stay, I'd get the degree out of the way and work with Dad as an electrician's mate in the holidays. I'd start looking at apprenticeship routes properly, even though it's not my first love. And I'd put every spare pound in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and some of it is grief. I do love reading, and it's strange to feel that thing might not matter anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is almost nothing. What would you do about the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot gap is a real thing for me. My dad's trade might hold until 2031, and so would the cafe. If I have to, I can work with my hands for a few years while things settle. I hadn't thought I'd want that, but there's pride in it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap for robots mean for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching might last longest of the thinking jobs, because kids need adults, but even that's not certain. I'd say plan for hands-on work and keep reading for love. If the degree is worthless as a job ticket, I'd rather have it as an education.

say: I'd say we need an **emergency plan**, with governments paying people to retrain.
I'd write something for the student paper.
think: Graduating in 2029 would feel like **finishing a race** after the stadium has been demolished.
I'd be gutted, and some of it is **grief**.
do: Talk with my parents about whether to **stay** on the degree.
Work as an **electrician's mate** with Dad in the holidays and look at apprenticeships.
feel: **Anxious**, partly grief, because I love reading and it may stop mattering.
S2.quote: Graduating in 2029 would feel like finishing a race after the stadium has been demolished.
fieldNote: The robot gap makes **hands-on** work feel like a real plan, not a joke.
Grief for the subject itself is unusual and honest.
Mood is anxious rather than alarmed because his dad's trade is a floor.

steps.text: Have a serious conversation with my parents about staying
Work holidays as an electrician's mate with Dad
Look into electrical apprenticeship routes properly
Save every spare pound from cafe shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time to prepare, and that universities should rewrite what they teach. I'd tell my friends to learn practical things as well as the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I could get a teaching job or a communications role for two or three years. That's not nothing, because teachers are valued. I'd probably be nervous, but I'd have a bit of padding by 2031. I'd also have to repay the loan from somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with the best mark I can manage, then do a teaching qualification. I'd take a part-time electrician's course in evenings, if I can afford it. I'd save a bit from my first salary, and learn the AI tools for lesson planning. And I'd keep the cafe job going until I land my first full-time post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy to anxious. I have time, and that stops it being a panic. But it's always there, like a train I can hear coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you graduation and a couple of working years. What do you do with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm a student when it hits and my family fallback is everything. With five years I'm earning, I've got a profession and savings. That makes it a problem I can plan for, not just survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is it different from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also think about moving abroad to teach, to see something before things change. That's the romantic bit. The sensible bit is staying near my parents and saving. I'd probably do the sensible one.

say: I'd say it's **enough time** to prepare and universities should rewrite what they teach.
I'd tell friends to learn practical things as well as books.
think: I could hold a **teaching** or communications job for two or three years, which is padding.
I'd still have to repay the **loan** from somewhere.
do: Finish the degree well, then take a **teaching qualification**.
Do an evening **electrician's course** if I can afford it.
Keep the **cafe job** until I land a first full-time post.
feel: **Uneasy** to anxious, like a train I can hear coming.
S3.quote: With five years I'm earning, I've got a profession and savings. That makes it a problem I can plan for, not just survive.
fieldNote: Time turns the problem into something **plannable**, and he says so directly.
Romantic idea of teaching abroad is weighed against sensible saving.
Evening electrical course shows his father's trade as a real second option.

steps.text: Complete a teaching qualification after the degree
Do an evening electrician's course if money allows
Keep cafe shifts until the first full-time post
Use AI tools for lesson planning in the first job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real gift, and we should use it to rebuild how we teach and work. I'd tell people the plan matters more than the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a lot calmer. A decade is a whole career stage. I could teach, maybe get a master's, and perhaps write something of my own. That's a good life, and I'd worry less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a normal route: degree, teaching qualification, a few years in a school, and maybe a master's in education. I'd put some money into a pension from the start. I'd keep up with the AI tools slowly, not rushing. And I'd write on the side, which was always the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly calm. Like knowing about a long road trip ahead, where you pack carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does it feel like a different picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's different because I could build a profession and a pension before anything hits. I'd also maybe have kids by then and I'd think about their schooling. That makes me care more about how schools change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who thinks that means they can relax?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to relax. Ten years goes quickly if you waste it, and everyone wastes the first few. I'd say learn something concrete every year, and keep a way of earning that doesn't rely on one employer.

say: I'd say it's a **real gift** and the plan matters more than the date.
I'd say we should use it to rebuild how we teach and work.
think: A decade is a **whole career stage**, enough to teach, study and write something of my own.
do: Complete **teaching qualification** and spend a few years in school.
Start a **pension** from the first payslip.
Learn the AI tools slowly and keep **writing** on the side.
feel: Uneasy but mostly **calm**, like a long road trip where you pack carefully.
S4.quote: Ten years goes quickly if you waste it, and everyone wastes the first few.
fieldNote: Time lets him keep his **love of writing** alongside a sensible profession.
Warns against complacency, which echoes his practical father.
Thinks ahead to children and schools, a longer view than most first-years.

steps.text: Finish a teaching qualification and work in a school
Open a pension from my first payslip
Write on the side and submit short pieces

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be locked into a degree that's about writing when the machines can write. What would help is retraining that doesn't bury me in debt, honest advice from the university, and a fallback like my dad's trade. Basically a way to switch without feeling I wasted three years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that humanities students aren't useless. We read, argue and write, and I think that's more than people give us credit for. If AI takes the writing, someone still needs to say what's true.

headlineQuote: If AI takes the writing, someone still needs to say what's true.
portrait: **Ben Ziegler** is 18, reading English literature and history, working at a station cafe, with an electrician father and council-worker mother.
He uses AI **now and then** for referencing but never lets it write.
His real worry is whether a **humanities degree** is worth the loan.
He drifts towards teaching, and his father's trade works as a quiet fallback.
He is uneasy in a plateau, anxious in the disruptive scenarios, and calmer with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries him most, locked into a writing degree while machines write.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **retraining** without heavy debt, honest university advice and a way to switch without wasting years.
